title: Access to recognized learning is becoming a distributional condition of adapting to digital, green, and demographic change
source_unit: ILO, Lifelong learning and skills for the future
geography: Global; cross-country institutional, labour-market, training, and online-vacancy evidence synthesized by the ILO

observations.period: 2026 report; global worker learning participation snapshot

denominator.unit: global worker learning-participation frame reported by the ILO

workers_receiving_training.unit: percent of all workers receiving training in the past year

full_time_permanent_formal_training.unit: percent of full-time permanent workers in formal firms receiving training

access_pattern.value: participation in structured learning is lowest among lower-educated, insecure, and small-enterprise workers

observations.method: ILO lifelong-learning report synthesis using new institutional and survey evidence, labour-market analysis, and cross-country comparisons; the participation figures are presented as broad comparative indicators rather than a single harmonized panel estimate.
observations.uncertainty: Country coverage, definitions of training, reference periods, formal/informal employment classifications, and survey methods may differ. The figures do not measure training quality, completion, skill recognition, wage return, or the same workers before and after training.
observations.subgroup: Workers by education, employment security, enterprise size, formality, sector, age, and access to recognized qualifications.
observations.counterinterpretation: Informal learning through day-to-day work, peer support, and practical experience is widespread but often invisible in formal indicators; low recorded training does not equal no learning, although unrecognized learning can still limit mobility.

observations.period: 2026 report; digital, green, and demographic transitions

denominator.unit: global skills-demand and transition frame assembled from labour-force and online-vacancy evidence

environmentally_relevant_tasks.unit: percent of workers already performing environmentally relevant tasks

long_term_care_demand.value: 85 million in 2023 to 158 million projected by 2050

rounded_skill_route.value: employers increasingly seek combinations of technical, digital, social, critical-thinking, and practical skills; rounded profiles are associated with better job characteristics

observations.method: ILO synthesis of online vacancy analysis, labour-force evidence, demographic projections, and policy research on skills for digitalization, the green transition, and care demand.
observations.uncertainty: Online vacancies do not represent all employers or jobs, and the reported association between rounded skills and better jobs is not a causal training estimate. Care-worker projections depend on demographic, service, financing, and occupational assumptions.
observations.subgroup: Workers and enterprises in digital, green, care, and other transforming sectors, including workers whose social-value skills are undervalued or weakly recognized.
observations.counterinterpretation: Skills supply alone cannot create decent work where infrastructure, industrial policy, employment institutions, care financing, or bargaining power are weak; higher demand may also coexist with low pay or poor conditions.

observations.period: 2026 report; public financing and institutional delivery

denominator.unit: countries with institutional data on adult-education allocation and lifelong-learning systems

low_adult_education_budget_high_income.unit: percent of high-income countries spending less than 1% of public education budgets on adult education

low_adult_education_budget_low_income.unit: percent of low-income countries spending less than 1% of public education budgets on adult education

delivery_constraints.value: fragmentation and weak implementation constrain cohesive lifelong-learning systems; governance, coordination, financing, and social dialogue are identified as success conditions

observations.method: ILO analysis of new institutional data from 21 countries and review of training-system evidence and policy implementation conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The budget shares are not a direct measure of per-worker spending, training quality, access, or outcomes. The 21-country institutional evidence is not a universal country ranking and does not establish that budget share alone determines system effectiveness.
observations.subgroup: Countries by income group, adult learners, disadvantaged workers, small enterprises, training providers, governments, employers, and workers' organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Small budget shares can coexist with effective employer, community, or work-based learning, while larger public allocations can fail when systems are fragmented or qualifications are not recognized. Delivery and local fit matter beyond funding totals.

boundary: This record adds an education-to-work-adaptation and institutional-delivery route. It is not respondent-level longitudinal data, does not estimate an individual training return, and does not establish that skills policy alone causes better wages, mobility, care quality, political participation, or geopolitical capacity.
